scenes.text: These are photographs from Mars. Ten small titanium tubes, lying on the ground, exactly where a robot put them.
Inside each one is a core of Martian rock, drilled and sealed by NASA's Perseverance rover.
And one of the tubes still on the rover holds something unusual. A rock with tiny dark spots, like the coat of a leopard.
The spots are made of two minerals that, on Earth, often form where microbes feed on mud and decaying organic matter.
In 2025, scientists described it as a potential biosignature. Not proof of life. A pattern that could have a biological origin. The rover can tell what the spots are made of. Not how they formed.
To find out what it really is, the rock has to come to Earth.
NASA had a plan to bring it here. Less than half a kilogram of rock, for an estimated eleven billion dollars.
That's more than twenty million dollars for every gram.
And in January 2026, the original programme lost its funding.
Which is strange, because we've done this before. In 1969, Apollo 11 brought back about twenty-two kilograms of the Moon.
And not only with astronauts. In 2024, a Chinese robot brought back samples from the far side of the Moon.
So why can we bring rocks back from the Moon, but not half a kilogram from Mars?
Start with the obvious difference. Mars is bigger. Its gravity is more than twice as strong as the Moon's.
To escape the Moon, you need about two point four kilometres per second. To escape Mars, about five.
That sounds like twice the effort. It's much worse.
If you've seen our video on getting to orbit, you know the rocket equation.
Fuel doesn't grow in step with speed. It grows exponentially, because extra fuel has to lift more fuel, too.
In a simple example, a small rocket leaving the Moon can be about half fuel. Leaving Mars, with the same kind of engine, about three quarters.
And that rocket has to get there first. Everything that launches from Mars has to land on Mars.
The Moon has no atmosphere at all. Mars has a thin one, just enough to burn you up, and too little for parachutes to stop you on their own.
NASA's planned lander would have weighed about two thousand three hundred kilograms. More than twice Perseverance. It would have been the heaviest thing ever landed on Mars.
Then it has to wait. Through dust storms, and nights of minus eighty degrees, for the samples to arrive.
The best launch windows come roughly every twenty-six months. Miss one, and the next is more than two years away.
And then it has to launch, with no one there. A radio signal from Earth takes between three and twenty-two minutes.
No rocket has ever launched from the surface of another planet. The Moon isn't a planet. A rocket launched from Mars would be the first.
So is it worth it?
After all, we already have pieces of Mars on Earth.
In 2025, the largest one ever found was sold at auction in New York. Twenty-four and a half kilograms of Martian rock.
It sold for five point three million dollars. About two hundred dollars a gram.
A hundred thousand times cheaper than the rock NASA wanted. So why not study meteorites?
Because a meteorite has no address.
It was blasted off Mars by an impact, drifted through space for millions of years, and burned through our atmosphere.
Then it lay in a desert. We don't know where on Mars it came from, what the impact did to it, or what Earth has added since.
That last part is not a detail. In 1996, scientists announced possible fossil microbes in a Martian meteorite from Antarctica.
It made headlines around the world. The debate lasted for decades. And it had spent thirteen thousand years in Antarctic ice, long enough for Earth to leave traces of its own.
The rocks in Perseverance's tubes are the opposite. We know exactly which layer each one came from.
And a rover can only do so much. Its instruments had to fit on a robot the size of a car, and survive a rocket launch.
On Earth, the samples could go to any laboratory in the world. Including ones with instruments that haven't been invented yet.
The rocks from Apollo are still being studied, more than fifty years later.
Some were kept sealed on purpose. In 2022, NASA opened a tube that astronauts had closed on the Moon in 1972, waiting for better tools.
So how did NASA plan to do it?
A rover would collect the tubes and bring them to the lander. A small rocket would carry them up, in a container the size of a basketball.
That rocket would weigh a few hundred kilograms. The rock inside, less than half a kilogram.
But it wouldn't fly home. It would only reach orbit around Mars.
There, a second spacecraft, to be built by the European Space Agency, would have to find the container, catch it, and carry it to Earth.
Why not just fly straight home?
A direct return would need a much bigger rocket, with enough fuel to escape Mars and head towards Earth. And that whole rocket, fuel and all, would have to land on Mars first.
Apollo faced the same choice. It left its return engine waiting in lunar orbit, and sent only a small lander down.
It's often imagined as catching a bullet. It isn't. Both spacecraft circle Mars together, barely moving relative to each other.
The hard part is everything before. The container doesn't steer. The orbiter has to find it, alone, in a very large sky.
Then approach and grab it, with no one on Earth able to step in.
A lander, a rover, a rocket, an orbiter, a capture system. Each one has to work the first time.
So the estimates kept climbing, review after review. Around four billion dollars in 2020. Later, seven. Then eleven, with the samples arriving no sooner than 2040.
Cheaper versions were drawn up. None of them was funded.
So what if we skipped all the handovers?
In 2024, NASA asked companies for new ideas. One of the seven studies it paid for came from SpaceX.
Its title was Enabling Mars Sample Return With Starship.
SpaceX shared few details. But the appeal is easy to see. Instead of several smaller machines, one very large spacecraft.
Imagine a ship big enough to combine several of these jobs. Landing, collecting samples, and eventually bringing them home.
But a ship that size needs a lot of fuel to leave Mars. Far too much to bring along.
So the idea is to make it there. The atmosphere is mostly carbon dioxide. Add hydrogen from water ice, and you can make methane.
Oxygen can be pulled from the carbon dioxide, too.
Perseverance has already tried that part. A small device called MOXIE made oxygen on Mars.
Over two years, in sixteen runs, it made a hundred and twenty-two grams. About what a small dog breathes in ten hours.
Now take a Starship with around twelve hundred tonnes of propellant, the figure usually quoted.
Most of that is oxygen. More than nine hundred tonnes.
That's more than seven million times what MOXIE made.
This isn't a test of Starship. MOXIE was never meant to fuel anything. It proved the chemistry works.
The gap is between a demonstration and a factory. And nobody has built that factory yet.
And even when the samples are on their way, the hardest decision may still be ahead.
How do you bring them down?
Scientists don't expect anything alive in those tubes. But nobody can prove there isn't.
So the rules are strict. Nothing from Mars should reach Earth outside a sealed container. And nothing from Earth should get in.
That second part matters just as much. Even a trace of Earth life could cloud the very question the mission was built to answer.
In NASA's original design, the capsule had no parachute.
A parachute is one more thing that can fail. So the capsule would simply fall into soft ground in the Utah desert,
at about a hundred and forty-five kilometres an hour. Built to survive the impact with the container intact.
And then the samples would go into a high-containment laboratory, to be checked before anyone else could touch them.
So where does that leave us now?
In November 2026, NASA took another look. Not with a mission, but with a team.
It starts work in January. Its recommendations are due around the end of 2027. There's no launch date, and no mission budget.
Meanwhile, China is building a mission of its own. It's called Tianwen-3.
Two rockets, around 2028. A lander with a small ascent rocket. An orbiter waiting above. A handover in Mars orbit.
NASA once planned a similar chain of spacecraft. The whole mission became too complex and too expensive.
China plans to bring back about half a kilogram of Mars, in 2031.
Is another space race coming?
We've learned to land on Mars, to drive there, to drill, even to fly. Coming back is a different problem.
We know what's waiting on Mars. The question is who will bring it home first.
So here's a question for you. If one of those tubes really did hold signs of ancient life, would it matter which country opened it? Let me know in the comments.
